title: How many Major Atlantic Hurricanes will occur in the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season?
resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as the number of major Atlantic hurricanes that occur between June 1, 2026, and November 30, 2026, inclusive, as reported by the [National Hurricane Center (NHC)](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/?atlc) of the United States National Weather Service on December 1, 2026.
fine_print: The question will be resolved using storm reports and data published by the National Hurricane Center as of December 1, 2026. Any subsequent revisions upgrading or downgrading a storm's intensity will not be considered. The NHC [Tropical Cyclone Advisory Archive](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/archive/2024/) and [Monthly Atlantic Tropical Weather Summary](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/text/MIATWSAT.shtml) may be used.
background:
The Atlantic hurricane season runs from June 1 to November 30, with peak activity occurring in August, September, and October. Major hurricanes, classified as Category 3 or higher on the [Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/aboutsshws.php), have sustained wind speeds of at least 111 miles per hour (178 km/h) and can cause significant damage and loss of life.

As of August 2026, no major hurricanes have taken place during the 2026 season, with only 4 named storms and a total [accumulated cyclone energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accumulated_cyclone_energy) of only 3.2.

On August 6, [NOAA released](https://www.cpc.ncep.noaa.gov/products/outlooks/hurricane.shtml) a forecast of a 70% probability for the following ranges:

* 7-13 Named Storms, including the 2 named storms that had been recorded to that point
* 2-6 Hurricanes
* 0-2 Major Hurricanes
* Accumulated Cyclone Energy (ACE) range of 30-90% of the median, including the 3% that had been recorded to that point

If fewer than 2 Major Hurricanes occur, it would be the fewest since 2013.

comments.author: DaiLothbrook
comments.text: I will start from a climatological mean of 3.29 major hurricanes, but the season-specific evidence now overwhelms that unconditional prior: the [NHC record ](\(https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/index.php?basin=atl\&season=2026\))shows six named storms, zero hurricanes, zero major hurricanes, and ACE roughly 93% below normal through 22 SeptemberSo, for the timebeing , I will move the probability of zero majors from 6% to 60% and reduce the expected total from 3.29 to about 0.55; I retain a meaningful 40% chance of at least one because late-September and October development remains climatologically possible, but four or more would require an extraordinary reversal in the remaining season.

comments.text:
This year has just set the record for the latest first hurricane of the season in the Atlantic, throughout all record-keeping, not just the satellite era (previously held by the 1941 season when the first hurricane formed on 9/17).

Assuming a hurricane does form eventually - if it doesn't, that record will probably have to be retired altogether.

comments.author: A6N23
comments.text:
The tropical Atlantic has been unusually quiet so far this season, so quiet that it just set a new record. 

There have been years when the season's first hurricane hasn't formed until September, with the "latest first hurricane" record set back in 2002 by Hurricane Gustav on Sept. 11 (later tied by Humberto in 2013).

The climatological peak of the Atlantic Hurricane season is on Sept. 10, a date we have surpassed.

The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season is below average at the beginning, this is because El Niño has been associated with calmer hurricane seasons, especially when predicted to be strong

The latest El Niño forecast now has a greater than 90% probability of becoming very strong, further limiting the potential for tropical development. This year's El Niño also has a greater than 75% chance of achieving record-breaking strength, according to NOAA.

comments.author: Koboh
comments.text:
I’m leaning toward 1 major hurricane. The season has been unusually quiet so far, with 5 named storms but no hurricanes and very low ACE by September 10. The strong El Nino and high wind shear make me think a big late season turnaround is less likely than usual. That said, I don’t think zero is a safe bet yet. September and October are still the main part of the Atlantic season, so there’s plenty of time for one storm to develop and intensify.

I’m roughly at **32% for 0, 48% for 1, 17% for 2, and 3% for 3+**. NOAA’s current outlook and CSU’s latest forecast also leave me more comfortable with **1 than 0 or 2+**.

So my best guess is 1 major hurricane, with zero still being a fairly close alternative.

My calculate chances **from today through November** end:

| Outcome             | My prediction |
| ------------------- | ------------- |
| 0 major hurricanes  | 32%           |
| 1 major hurricane   | 48%           |
| 2 major hurricanes  | 17%           |
| 3 major hurricanes  | 2.5%          |
| 4+ major hurricanes | 0.5%          |



**Why I’m favoring 1 rather than 0 or 2+**

The main reason I’m leaning toward **1 major hurricane** is the unusually quiet starting point. As of September 10, the Atlantic has produced only 5 named storms, with no hurricanes and just 4.4 ACE. That’s roughly 92% below the 1991–2020 average for this point in the season.

Given how suppressed the season has been so far, I find it difficult to see a sudden shift toward a run of multiple major hurricanes. The broader atmospheric pattern also makes a major turn around less likely. NOAA expects the strong El Nino to continue, and the associated increase in vertical wind shear remains one of the biggest obstacles to sustained Atlantic development.

At the same time, I don’t think the current inactivity is enough to justify going with **zero**. September and October still contain a large portion of the season’s climatological activity, and Atlantic conditions can change surprisingly quickly when the shorter term environment becomes more favorable. NOAA has also pointed out that these shorter term weather patterns can persist for weeks and have a significant influence on how the rest of the season unfolds.

So, for me 1 major hurricane sits in the middle ground. The season has been far too quiet so far for me to confidently expect 2 or more, but there is still enough of the peak season ahead and enough potential for the pattern to temporarily improve that I’m not ready to call it a zero either.
